_note: Human reference data used as calibration targets or predictions. 'verified' = read in the primary source during this project; 'secondary' = only from secondary summaries — verify before publishing.

ebbinghaus_savings.source: Murre & Dros (2015), Replication and Analysis of Ebbinghaus' Forgetting Curve, PLoS ONE 10(7): e0120644, Table 3 (Ebbinghaus column, from his 1880 manuscript p. 56). Plotted intervals per the paper: 19 min, 63 min, 8.75 h, 1 d, 2 d, 6 d, 31 d.
ebbinghaus_savings.measure: savings (proportion of original learning time saved on relearning) — a retention proxy, not recall probability

dros_savings.source: Murre & Dros (2015), Table 3, replication (single subject, Dros).

drm_rm1995_exp2_recognition.source: Roediger & McDermott (1995), Creating false memories, JEP:LMC 21(4), 803-814, Experiment 2, Table 2 (proportion 'old'). We use the study + arithmetic condition (no prior recall), which matches our memory-level test.

drm_rm1995_exp2_recall.source: Roediger & McDermott (1995), Experiment 2, Figure 3 caption and Results.

drm_rm1995_exp1_recognition.source: Roediger & McDermott (1995), Experiment 1, Table 1 (ratings 3 or 4 = old; after free recall).

loftus_palmer_1974_broken_glass.source: Loftus & Palmer (1974), J. Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior 13, 585-589, Experiment 2 — 'Did you see any broken glass?' (there was none).

loftus_miller_burns_1978.source: Loftus, Miller & Burns (1978), Semantic integration of verbal information into a visual memory, JEP: Human Learning and Memory 4, 19-31. Figures below are from secondary summaries; the qualitative timing pattern is the target.
loftus_miller_burns_1978.timing_pattern: Misleading information is most damaging when it arrives late in a long retention interval (original memory weak, misinformation fresh).
